subject: Can OccuRN work for single sites?

messages.author: 82f218c513e6c73a
messages.subject: Can OccuRN work for single sites?
parts:
Good afternoon,

I am trying to estimate bird abundances for my study area across a single season. I have detected/ non-detected data of over 100 species across 50 different sampling events, but it all took place at the same location within a single site.
Essentially my data looks like this, only x 100 :

Species      Survey1  Survey2   Survey3...
Species1              1            0            1...
Species2              0            1            1...
...

What I would like to do is get an estimate of each species' abundance for this site. I've tried to run a model for a single species individually using a matrix such as above but one row at a time but get this error: 

birdsp1 <- read.csv("C:/Users/Jody/Desktop/Birds.csv",  sep =";", header = TRUE)
> UMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(birdsp1)
> Model <- occuRN (~ 1 ~ 1, UMF)

Error in base::rowSums(x, na.rm = na.rm, dims = dims, ...) : 
  'x' must be an array of at least two dimensions

Now I know this is because there is only a single row in the matrix, but since I only have a single site I'm not sure how to work around this. What could I do to correct this? Am I using the incorrect model and if so which should I be using? I have tried to base my analyses on this paper: Effectiveness of protected areas for bird conservation dependson guild. Divers Distrib. 2018;24:1083–1091.

Thanks, 

Jody.

messages.author: 82f218c513e6c73a
messages.subject: Re: Can OccuRN work for single sites?
parts:
Okay so a potential workaround to this problem includes adding a row of NA values under each species. This allows the model to run but unfortunately does not allow for the use of bayesian estimates via ranef later. What does work to get abundance is the use of backtransform or predict. So my code now looks as follows

library(unmarked)
birds <- read.csv("Birds.csv", sep = ";")

# Take the first species and harvest the detection data by columns
# Add in one too many rows so it can be filled in with NAS
species1 <-birds[1:2, 2:18] ##
species1 [2,] <- NA

# Put it into the umf
umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=species1)

# Run the model
mod1 <- occuRN(~1 ~1, data=umf)

# Abundance
backTransform(mod1, "state")

#Detectability
backTransform(mod1, "det")

########################################

parts:
For the examples I've tried using your technique of adding in an extra row of NA values, I get values for abundance but NA's for detectability and all of the standard errors.  If that isn't your experience, I'll go back to the drawing board to see what I'm doing wrong.

But if not...So while I think one should almost always use a package written by someone else as that package will usually be (at least for me) far more robust and logical that anything I could write - and that especially goes for unmarked, I think you or one of us will need to write code for this as the estimates of standard errors are essential.

If I understand correctly the only two pieces of relevant information for each species are the number of visits (around 50) and the number of detections.  (I'd label the number of detections as the sufficient statistic to estimate both abundance and detectability (assuming that there are no other covariates.)

Anyway...if you're not getting standard errors, please let me know and I'll work on this a bit more.

Jim

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Can OccuRN work for single sites?
parts:
Hi Jody,

I think Jim's first instinct might be right--it doesn't seem possible that the model is identifiable with one 'site', and I think this is why the occuRN function expects multiple rows.  I think you're getting an answer that depends upon where you choose to stop the integration over the latent abundance state and where you end up starting the optimizer.

library(unmarked)
y<-matrix(NA, 2, 50)
y[1, ]<-rbinom(50, 1, 1-(1-.2)^5) ##N is 5, r = 0.2 
UMF<-unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y)
rn<-occuRN(~1 ~1, UMF)
predict(rn, "state")
rn2<-occuRN(~1 ~1, UMF, K=100)
rn2_5<-occuRN(~1 ~1, UMF, K=100, starts=c(2, -3))
rn2_5_5<-occuRN(~1 ~1, UMF, K=100, starts=c(0, 1))
predict(rn2, "state")
predict(rn2_5, "state")
predict(rn2_5_5, "state")
rn3<-occuRN(~1 ~1, UMF, K=1000)
predict(rn3, "state")


The model needs some 'site' replication to tease the state/detection processes apart. That said, there's some wiggle room w/r/t how sites are defined---here's an example where different years at one site are treated as different 'sites'', and splitting your sampling periods up *might* be one way to tackle this. (Another way might be to treat each species as a 'site'', although this also raises a different set of issues). If you have recorded times of detection, or distances, there might be better options available to you.

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Can OccuRN work for single sites?
parts:
I've attached a write-up which suggests (as does John Clare) that either the model is not identifiable or it is "nearly not identifiable" (a term that I obviously made up).  Here is the first part of the write-up:

Jody found an ingenious work-around for getting occuRN to produce estimates and standard errors when there is but a single site by adding in a second row of NA values.  However, while Jody’s approach does produce results, these are not the values of the maximum likelihood estimates.

But following Jody’s lead by having the second row of data being a duplicate of the first row (instead of putting in NA’s) gets one the maximum likelihood estimates with the standard errors inflated by a multiplicative factor of the square root of 2 if the starting values are close enough to the maximum likelihood estimates.

First the logic:  By having two rows of identical data just doubles the log of the likelihood (or squares the likelihood).  Therefore, the values that maximize twice the log of the likelihood will not have changed from using the log of the likelihood for a single site.  This also implies that the resulting variances will be underestimated by a multiplicative factor of 2.

A teaser:  Below I suggest that for a single site maximum likelihood estimates are useless. 

And here is a look at the log likelihood surface when T=17, w=10, and K=100:

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Can OccuRN work for single sites?
parts:
Below are contour plots of the log likelihood surface showing that for a single site the maximum likelihood estimate of abundance is much greater than 10,000 and the detection probability less than 0.0001 for two scenarios with an infinite value for K: T=17 and w=10 and T=50 and w=25.  It would not be surprising if the actual maximum likelihood values are infinity and 0 for lambda and p, respectively.

The conclusion seems to be that for single sites (and for multiple sites with the same number of visits and detections), maximum likelihood does not produce plausible or useful results.

Jim
